lines.text: Last time we left two keys sitting right on top of each other, in the exact same slot, with no idea what happens next.
That's not a bug in the hash function. The hash function already did its job — it just never promised this couldn't happen.
So here's the oldest answer anyone gave to that problem, and it's still the one most standard libraries start with.
Here's the whole trick, and it's smaller than it looks: a bucket stops being one slot for one entry.
It becomes the head of a list. Every new key that lands there just gets linked on.
And notice what I didn't have to build to make that work — it's the exact same singly-linked list from two chapters back. Nothing new, just reused in a new place.
I want you to see this isn't a textbook simplification before we go any further.
This is Java's own source comment, word for word: a binned, bucketed hash table. That's chaining, shipping in one of the most used libraries on earth.
One honest footnote, though — once a bucket gets big enough, Java quietly upgrades it to a balanced tree instead of a plain list. Hold onto that; it'll matter again later.

lines.text: Before I show you the real measurement, make a prediction.
At a load factor around one and a half — more keys than buckets — how long is the chain a typical key probably lands in?
It's about alpha itself — the load factor, nothing fancier.
n divided by m is exactly what alpha means, so a random key's expected chain length tracks that same ratio.
Now push this mechanism as far as it can go, on purpose. What if every single key happened to land in the same bucket?
Watch the chain just keep growing. Access time slides toward scanning the whole thing — order n, the same cost as never hashing at all.
But notice what doesn't happen: nothing breaks. There's no fixed capacity per bucket to overflow — it just gets slow.

lines.text: Here's the citation, straight from the lecture: expected search cost is theta of one plus alpha.
Now watch the part that should actually give you pause. The average chain length equals alpha, exactly, every single time I measure it — true no matter how bad the hash function is.
Even a hash that sends everything to one bucket gets that same average, by simple counting.

So the average alone proves nothing. What actually matters is whether the longest chain stays near that average instead of hoarding every key — and that's the one thing a well-spread hash genuinely buys you.
One more cost before we move on, and it's the one worth remembering.
Every node in this chain is carrying a pointer to the next one. That pointer isn't free — it's memory you're spending on bookkeeping, not on the key itself.
Next topic gives that pointer up entirely, by storing every entry directly inside the table. It pays for that a completely different way.
Three load factors, one real table, built fresh each time — nothing here is simulated.
Watch the average track alpha almost perfectly at all three, exactly as the counting argument guarantees.
And watch the longest chain stay a small fraction of the total, every time — next to the worst case on the right, where one single chain is holding everything.
